entries.name: Tirzepatide Franchise (Mounjaro / Zepbound)
entries.thesisShort: Eli Lilly's tirzepatide is the world's best-selling drug in 2025, with Zepbound holding ~70% of new branded obesity scripts and Mounjaro leading diabetes incretins on both sides of the Atlantic.
entries.thesisLong:
Lilly is the single most important chokepoint in the GLP-1 era. Tirzepatide became the world's top-selling drug in Q3 2025, and the combined Mounjaro+Zepbound franchise drove roughly 56% of Lilly's revenue. Q4 2025 Mounjaro worldwide revenue grew 110% to $7.4B and US Zepbound grew 122% YoY, putting the franchise on a multi-tens-of-billions annualized run rate.

The moat is dual-mechanism. Tirzepatide's GLP-1/GIP dual agonism delivers superior weight loss versus Novo's semaglutide in head-to-head trials, and Lilly's oral orforglipron is on track to be the first oral small-molecule GLP-1 with submission and launch in 2026 — a manufacturing and distribution unlock that injectables can't match.

Capacity is the bottleneck. Lilly is spending $50B+ on US manufacturing (Concord NC, Lebanon IN, Mount Pleasant NC, Houston TX, plus a new $3B site announced in Q3 2025) to relieve API and fill-finish constraints. Even with the build-out, demand still outstrips supply for higher-dose Zepbound vials.

2026 guidance of $80–83B revenue with Lilly set to lead pharma by revenue in 2026 reflects how far ahead the franchise sits. Risks are concentrated: a single safety signal, accelerated Medicare price negotiation, or Viking/Amgen approvals each compress the moat — but on the question of who gates the obesity supercycle in 2026, the answer is Lilly.
catalysts: Orforglipron oral GLP-1 FDA submission and 2026 launch
Mount Pleasant and Houston API plant qualifications
Tirzepatide HFpEF, OSA, and MASH label expansions
Retatrutide (triple agonist) Phase 3 readouts
Direct-to-consumer LillyDirect channel scaling
risks: Medicare IRA price negotiation reaching tirzepatide
Compounded GLP-1 reintroduction if shortage list returns
Viking VK2735 or Amgen MariTide encroaching
Adverse safety signal in long-duration outcomes data

entries.name: Semaglutide Franchise (Ozempic / Wegovy)
entries.thesisShort: Novo Nordisk still owns roughly 60% of branded obesity GLP-1 volume globally and used the $16.5B Catalent deal to vertically integrate three fill-finish sites that gate Wegovy and Ozempic supply.
entries.thesisLong:
Novo is the incumbent GLP-1 power. 2025 Wegovy sales reached DKK 79.1B and Ozempic DKK 127.1B, with obesity care growing 26% in DKK and the company maintaining a 59.6% branded volume share in obesity GLP-1s. Even after Lilly's tirzepatide caught up on weight-loss efficacy, Novo's installed prescriber base and DTC machine kept semaglutide growing.

The Catalent transaction is the structural story. Novo Holdings closed the $16.5B Catalent acquisition and routed three fill-finish sites (Anagni Italy, Brussels Belgium, Bloomington Indiana) to Novo Nordisk in an $11B sub-deal. Brussels capacity is set to double to 100–150M vials/year and Indiana adds another 70M vials, with first-volume contribution beginning in 2026 — the structural fix to the multi-year supply shortage.

Novo also slashed US GLP-1 prices up to 70% in late 2025 to widen access and head off compounders, but management still expects 2026 semaglutide revenue to hold or grow on volume. The Akero acquisition layered on a MASH thesis adjacent to the obesity franchise.

The risk is Lilly. Tirzepatide's efficiency edge and orforglipron's oral path narrowed Novo's lead, and CagriSema's mixed Phase 3 readout in late 2025 dented the next-gen story. But the installed manufacturing footprint, the Catalent vertical integration, and 60% share of branded obesity make Novo a permanent fixture in the GLP-1 chokepoint map.
catalysts: Catalent fill-finish ramp into 2026 Wegovy supply
Oral semaglutide 25mg obesity launch progression
Akero MASH portfolio integration
Kalundborg and Clayton API expansions online
Medicare and Medicaid GLP-1 access expansion
risks: Lilly tirzepatide and orforglipron share gains
CagriSema next-gen disappointment
Pricing concessions compress gross margin
Compounding reentry if FDA shortage list reactivates

entries.name: VK2735 Dual GLP-1/GIP Agonist
entries.thesisShort: Viking is the most credible third entrant in the GLP-1 race, with both subcutaneous and oral VK2735 in Phase 3 and a maintenance-dosing differentiation that could carve out a unique slot.
entries.thesisLong:
Viking Therapeutics is the merchant disruptor in the GLP-1 duopoly. VK2735 is a dual GLP-1/GIP agonist with two Phase 3 obesity trials underway: VANQUISH-1 (obesity, enrollment complete) and VANQUISH-2 (obesity + T2D, enrollment completed March 2026). Both are 78-week subcutaneous studies that should read out in 2027.

The oral story is what differentiates Viking from a generic biosimilar threat. The Phase 2 VENTURE-Oral trial showed 12% weight loss with the tablet formulation, and Viking has guided to advancing oral VK2735 into Phase 3 in Q3 2026 — a credible path to becoming the first oral dual agonist on market and a real competitive threat to Lilly's orforglipron.

A third differentiator is the Maintenance Dosing study with results expected Q3 2026, exploring monthly dosing or subcutaneous-to-oral transition for weight maintenance. If clean, that opens a unique label position no other GLP-1 player can match.

The risk is binary: Viking is single-asset and pre-revenue, the cap table is heavily diluted by R&D spend, and any safety or efficacy stumble in VANQUISH could collapse the equity. But on the bottleneck question — who breaks the GLP-1 duopoly first — VK2735 is the asset most likely to do it.
catalysts: VANQUISH-1 and VANQUISH-2 Phase 3 readouts in 2027
Oral VK2735 Phase 3 initiation Q3 2026
Maintenance dosing Phase 2 results Q3 2026
Potential M&A premium from large-cap buyer
VK0214 X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy program updates
risks: Single-asset binary execution risk
Lilly orforglipron oral approval first-to-market
Manufacturing partner scarcity at commercial scale
Capital raise dilution before launch

entries.name: Sterile Fill-Finish Capacity
entries.thesisShort: With Catalent taken private by Novo Holdings, Thermo Fisher's Patheon sterile network is now the largest listed independent representative of the fill-finish chokepoint — the binding constraint on how many GLP-1 pens and injectable-biologic vials reach patients.
entries.thesisLong:
Sterile fill-finish — filling drug substance into vials, syringes, and pens under aseptic conditions — is the textbook injectable-biologics bottleneck, and the public representative shifted in 2024. Novo Holdings took Catalent private for $16.5B and Novo Nordisk absorbed its three marquee sites (Anagni IT, Brussels BE, Bloomington IN) for $11B, removing the sector's largest merchant fill-finish name from public markets. Thermo Fisher Scientific (TMO), through its Patheon sterile drug-product network, is now the largest listed independent representative of this chokepoint.

The industry context is unchanged: GLP-1 demand outpaced sterile injectable fill-finish capacity by 2–3x for two consecutive years, and Patheon, Lonza, Samsung Biologics, and the former Catalent sites all sat on multi-year backlogs, with aseptic fill lead times still routinely exceeding a year at peak. Thermo Fisher has been expanding sterile fill-finish across its Patheon footprint to absorb spillover demand as Novo internalizes its own semaglutide volume.

The structural lesson holds: fill-finish, not API synthesis, is the binding constraint for injectable biologics — and any listed CDMO with proven sterile fill capacity (Thermo Fisher / Patheon most prominently, with Lonza and Samsung Biologics on foreign exchanges) is effectively a long-dated royalty on the GLP-1 and biologics build-out.

For portfolio purposes the cleanest vertically integrated public proxies remain LLY and NVO themselves, with WST supplying the elastomer components in every pen. Thermo Fisher is a diversified tools-and-CDMO conglomerate, so Patheon fill-finish is one line within a much larger story rather than a pure play.
catalysts: Patheon sterile fill-finish capacity expansions absorbing spillover demand
GLP-1 and injectable-biologics volume growth into 2026
Annex 1 reinvestment cycle lifting demand for high-spec aseptic fill
Biosimilar and ADC launches broadening sterile fill pipelines
Sterile injectable pricing firm on multi-year backlogs
risks: GLP-1 demand surprise to the downside after price cuts
Patheon fill-finish is a small slice of a diversified TMO conglomerate
Novo internalizing volume reduces merchant CDMO demand

entries.name: Bioprocessing Consumables & Filtration
entries.thesisShort: Repligen sells the disposable bags, filters, and Protein A resins that every monoclonal antibody and cell therapy facility consumes by the kilogram — a recurring-revenue toll on the entire biologics buildout.
entries.thesisLong:
Repligen sits inside every modern biologics suite. The company makes Protein A affinity resins (chromatography purification of mAbs), tangential flow filters, single-use bioprocessing bags, and analytics — the high-touch consumables that scale linearly with biologics output. After the post-COVID destock, the business returned to growth: 2025 revenue was $738M, +16% YoY (reported and organic ex-COVID), with 14% organic growth in Q4 2025 led by Analytics and Proteins.

The FlexBiosys acquisition (2025) vertically integrated single-use bags and assemblies into the systems portfolio — closing the gap with Sartorius and Cytiva on full-flow single-use offerings. Cross-selling to large biopharma and CDMO accounts continues to be the operating leverage story.

Structural tailwinds: ADC pipeline expansion (Pfizer/Seagen, AstraZeneca/Daiichi), GLP-1 capacity build-out, cell and gene therapy commercialization (Casgevy, CAR-T expansions), and biosimilar wave entering manufacturing all push consumables demand higher. Bioprocessing is back on a 10–12% medium-term CAGR after the COVID hangover cleared.

The risk is customer concentration in the CDMO channel and the fact that Sartorius, Cytiva (Danaher), and Thermo are all larger and can bundle. But Repligen's pure-play exposure and Protein A franchise (where it's the merchant leader) make it the cleanest public name on the bioprocessing-consumables chokepoint.
catalysts: ADC manufacturing buildout driving filter/resin demand
GLP-1 process intensification orders
Cell & gene therapy commercial launches
FlexBiosys cross-sell into large CDMO accounts
Biosimilar wave hitting US in 2026-2028
risks: Sartorius / Cytiva / Thermo bundling competition
CDMO customer destocking cycles
China biopharma exposure under BIOSECURE-type rules

entries.name: GLP-1 Elastomer & Containment Components
entries.thesisShort: West makes the elastomer stoppers, plungers, and seals inside every GLP-1 pen and vial — a quiet ~9% revenue line that grows in lockstep with Wegovy, Zepbound, and the broader injectable biologics surge.
entries.thesisLong:
West Pharmaceutical Services is the picks-and-shovels play on injectables. Its proprietary elastomer components (NovaPure, FluroTec, Westar) seal essentially every prefilled syringe, autoinjector, and lyophilized vial in modern biologics, and GLP-1 pens are now a measurable single-product line: GLP-1 elastomer parts hit ~9% of company revenue in Q3 2025, up from ~8% in Q2.

The capital plan is sized to the opportunity: West is spending $350–400M in 2025 on high-value product (HVP) capacity, with key build-outs at Waterford Ireland and Kinston North Carolina aimed at GLP-1 components and premium elastomers. EU GMP Annex 1 sterile manufacturing rules are simultaneously forcing customers to upgrade to higher-spec components, lifting mix.

Past the GLP-1 wave, West has an embedded structural tailwind: every new biologic launches in injectable form, every autoinjector has 3–7 West parts, and the qualified-supplier list at Tier 1 pharma is short. Switching costs are high because primary container changes require regulatory filings.

The risk is execution on the HVP buildouts (Annex 1 capex is back-loaded) and customer destocking after the COVID-era over-order. But on the GLP-1 chokepoint map, West sits alongside Catalent and the API players as a name that physically gates how many pens ship in 2026.
catalysts: Waterford and Kinston capacity online for 2026 GLP-1
Annex 1 driven HVP mix shift acceleration
ADC and biologics launches expanding container demand
Biosimilar wave requiring new container qualifications
Auto-injector adoption in oncology and immunology
risks: GLP-1 destock cycle from over-ordered customers
Capex execution risk on Annex 1 expansions
Customer concentration with Lilly and Novo

entries.name: Casgevy Gene Therapy & Rare Disease Franchise
entries.thesisShort: Vertex is the dominant cash-generating gene therapy commercial machine, ramping Casgevy through ~300 patient initiations in 2025 while leveraging cystic fibrosis cash flow into rare disease and pain.
entries.thesisLong:
Vertex is unique in biotech: a profitable, growing rare-disease franchise (cystic fibrosis with Trikafta/Kaftrio) that funds an aggressive expansion into gene therapy, sickle cell, type 1 diabetes, and non-opioid pain (Journavx). Casgevy — the first approved CRISPR gene therapy — initiated cell collections in roughly 300 patients in 2025, with 150 first cell collections and 64 infusions in Q4 alone. That 2025 ramp nearly tripled 2024.

The bottleneck is real and it's not pricing. Casgevy requires myeloablative conditioning, hospital-grade authorized treatment centers, and weeks of inpatient time per patient — capacity sits at the ATC/hospital level, not at Vertex. Vertex has been investing in ATC qualification and patient navigation to widen the funnel; William Blair models 2026 Casgevy revenue at ~$344M with Vertex taking ~$212M.

The pediatric expansion is the next unlock. Vertex completed enrollment in the 5–11 SCD/TDT studies and plans global filings in H1 2026, including a US sBLA. England reimbursement was secured in 2025; access in MENA and other ex-US markets continues to broaden.

The equity story extends well beyond Casgevy: vanzacaftor triplet (next-gen CF), Journavx for acute pain (NaV1.8 inhibitor), zimislecel for type 1 diabetes islet replacement, and inaxaplin for APOL1 kidney disease all sit in late-stage. The risk is Casgevy's slow ramp continues to disappoint, but the diversified pipeline gives Vertex more shots on goal than any pure-play gene therapy peer.
catalysts: Pediatric SCD/TDT global regulatory submissions H1 2026
ATC capacity additions widening patient funnel
Journavx (suzetrigine) commercial ramp in acute pain
Vanzacaftor triplet share gains in CF
Zimislecel pivotal data in type 1 diabetes
risks: Casgevy ramp continues to disappoint on hospital bottleneck
Suzetrigine label competition vs opioids
CF franchise erosion if HHS pricing concessions accelerate

entries.name: In Vivo CRISPR Editing Pipeline
entries.thesisShort: CRISPR Therapeutics owns the platform side of Casgevy plus the most advanced in vivo CRISPR pipeline, with three LNP-delivered editors entering or running clinical trials in 2026.
entries.thesisLong:
CRISPR Therapeutics is the platform-level beneficiary of Casgevy and the leading independent in vivo gene editor. CASGEVY contributed $100M of total program revenue in 2025 to CRSP, with the share of commercial economics expected to grow as Vertex scales infusions in 2026 and adds the pediatric label.

The in vivo pipeline is what makes CRSP a distinct asset versus Vertex. CTX310 (LNP-delivered ANGPTL3 editor for triglycerides and LDL) showed durable lipid lowering after a single IV dose, with updates expected H2 2026. CTX340 (refractory hypertension via AGT editing) showed >90% AGT reduction in NHPs and enters clinical testing H1 2026. CTX460 (alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency in vivo correction) starts clinical mid-2026.

The strategic prize is in vivo editing of hematopoietic stem cells, which would replace Casgevy's ex vivo workflow with a single IV infusion and collapse the ATC bottleneck entirely. CRSP is actively developing an LNP-based HSC editing approach for SCD/TDT — speculative but transformational if it works.

The risk profile is high: in vivo editing has had safety setbacks across the field (Intellia, Beam, Verve), the LNP delivery science is unforgiving, and CRSP's cash runway depends on Casgevy royalties scaling on schedule. But the breadth of in vivo programs combined with the embedded Casgevy stake makes CRSP the most diversified merchant CRISPR equity.

chokepointMetrics.label: In vivo programs in clinic by mid-2026

catalysts: CTX310 Phase 1 update H2 2026
CTX340 first-in-human dosing in refractory hypertension
Casgevy pediatric label expansion driving royalties
In vivo HSC editing IND filing (SCD/TDT)
Potential platform deal or partnership
risks: In vivo CRISPR safety event across the field
LNP delivery limitations to non-liver tissues
Casgevy ramp slower than expected hits royalties

entries.name: Post-Keytruda Oncology Pipeline
entries.thesisShort: Merck's Keytruda hit ~$31.7B in 2025 sales as the world's top-selling drug, but with US LOE in December 2028 the entire equity now hinges on whether the post-Keytruda pipeline can replace $30B+ of revenue.
entries.thesisLong:
Merck is the cleanest LOE-cliff trade in big pharma. Keytruda generated nearly $31.7B in 2025 (+7% YoY) and accounts for ~55% of Merck's pharmaceutical sales. Management expects peak sales of $35B by 2028, with US revenue starting to decline in January 2028 (IRA pricing) and falling sharply after the December 2028 compound patent expiry. EU LOE follows in 2031.

The defense plan rests on a portfolio of 20+ growth drivers Merck claims hold blockbuster potential: $25B+ in oncology, $20B+ in cardiometabolic, $15B+ in infectious disease. Subcutaneous Keytruda (extended IP runway), Winrevair (pulmonary arterial hypertension, acquired via Acceleron), Capvaxive (pneumococcal vaccine), Welireg (VHL/RCC), and the late-stage ADC pipeline acquired through partnerships (Daiichi Sankyo collaboration on ADCs) form the bridge.

Merck split oncology into a standalone business unit in late 2025 to focus operational accountability on the post-Keytruda oncology portfolio. The Phase 3 pipeline has nearly tripled since 2021 through internal advancement and M&A.

The bet is execution: management guides to $70B+ of non-risk-adjusted commercial opportunity by mid-2030s, but every analyst model assumes meaningful pipeline failures. The chokepoint dimension is that Keytruda is itself the global standard-of-care immunotherapy backbone — combinations with Keytruda are how almost every new I-O asset is tested. Loss of that anchor is a generational test for big pharma R&D.
catalysts: Subcutaneous Keytruda launch extending IP
Winrevair PAH label expansion to earlier lines
Daiichi-partnered ADC Phase 3 readouts
Welireg label expansions in solid tumors
M&A to backfill pipeline gaps
risks: Keytruda biosimilar entry timing in US 2028-2029
Pipeline blockbuster failures (PD-1/VEGF combos, etc.)
IRA price negotiation broadening to oncology

entries.name: Seagen ADC Portfolio & Oncology Reset
entries.thesisShort: Pfizer's $43B Seagen acquisition doubled the oncology pipeline to 60 programs and 12 ADCs, anchored by four approved vedotin medicines that are scaling into broader indications across 2025-2026.
entries.thesisLong:
Pfizer's oncology strategy is now Seagen plus everything else. The $43B Seagen acquisition doubled the oncology clinical pipeline to 60 programs across ADCs, small molecules, bispecifics, and immunotherapies, with 12 ADCs now in development across four payload classes (vedotin, TOPO1 inhibitor, next-gen auristatin, and novel mechanisms).

The four approved Seagen-origin ADCs anchor the commercial story: ADCETRIS (brentuximab vedotin) in Hodgkin lymphoma, PADCEV (enfortumab vedotin) in urothelial cancer, TIVDAK (tisotumab vedotin) in cervical cancer, and TUKYSA (tucatinib) in HER2+ breast and colorectal. Combined with Pfizer's legacy Ibrance (CDK4/6), Xtandi (prostate), and Lorbrena (lung), the oncology portfolio now spans 25+ approved medicines and biosimilars across 40+ indications.

The 2025-2026 catalysts focus on late-stage assets: sigvotatug vedotin is in Phase 3 for NSCLC with data anticipated in 2025-2026, and atirmociclib (next-gen CDK4-selective inhibitor) is advancing in HR+ breast cancer. Padcev's expansion into earlier-line urothelial use is broadening the franchise materially.

The risk is execution and integration: Seagen's burn was material, ADC-class ILD safety overhang from Daiichi's Enhertu colors investor confidence in all ADC platforms, and Pfizer's overall revenue base is still recovering from the post-COVID step-down. But on the chokepoint question of who gates ADC innovation outside Daiichi, Pfizer-Seagen is the clearest answer in big pharma.
catalysts: Sigvotatug vedotin Phase 3 NSCLC readout
Padcev earlier-line urothelial expansion
Atirmociclib (CDK4-selective) Phase 3 progression
Elrexfio (BCMA bispecific) multiple myeloma growth
Vepdegestrant (PROTAC SERD) advancement
risks: ADC-class ILD safety scrutiny
Seagen integration execution
Ibrance and Xtandi LOE pressure approaching

entries.name: Post-Eliquis / Opdivo Growth Portfolio
entries.thesisShort: BMY's Eliquis and Opdivo together drove ~$24.5B (51% of revenue) in 2025 but face EU Eliquis generics in May 2026 and US Opdivo LOE in 2028, forcing a pivot to a 60%-of-revenue growth portfolio led by Breyanzi, Camzyos, and Reblozyl.
entries.thesisLong:
Bristol-Myers Squibb is the LOE-vs-pipeline trade. Eliquis (anticoagulant) and Opdivo (PD-1) generated combined worldwide sales of $24.5B in 2025 — 51% of revenue. Eliquis loses US exclusivity in 2026 with EU generic entry already starting in May 2026, and Opdivo LOE follows in 2028 (US), 2030 (EU), 2031 (Japan).

The defense is the growth portfolio, now approaching ~60% of total revenue. Key assets: Breyanzi (CAR-T for LBCL/CLL/follicular), Camzyos (cardiac myosin inhibitor in obstructive HCM), Opdualag (PD-1 + LAG-3 fixed-dose combo in melanoma), Reblozyl (anemia in MDS/beta-thal), Sotyktu (TYK2 in psoriasis), Cobenfy (KarXT acquired via Karuna for schizophrenia and now Alzheimer's psychosis trials).

Management describes the pipeline as the richest in a decade, with up to 12 late-stage readouts across eight assets. Recent Opdivo wins include the cHL combination approval and expanded perioperative NSCLC use — extending Opdivo's lifetime even with the patent clock running.

The risk profile is heavy: Eliquis erosion is faster than initially modeled, the growth portfolio still needs to absorb $20B+ of revenue replacement in 4 years, and FY2026 guidance was cautious. But on the bottleneck map, BMY's CAR-T (Breyanzi), cardiac myosin (Camzyos), and TYK2 (Sotyktu) franchises each occupy distinct chokepoints with limited direct competition.
catalysts: Breyanzi label expansions and outpatient access growth
Camzyos non-obstructive HCM Phase 3 readout
Cobenfy Alzheimer's psychosis Phase 3 data
Opdivo perioperative NSCLC expansion
Reblozyl first-line MDS launch
risks: Eliquis revenue cliff steeper than guided
Cobenfy Alzheimer's data disappointment
Slower-than-modeled growth portfolio ramp

entries.name: Continuous Glucose Monitoring (CGM)
entries.thesisShort: Dexcom owns ~74% US CGM share with $4.66B in 2025 revenue, and the G7 15-Day system plus over-the-counter Stelo extend the franchise into Type 2 diabetes and the prediabetic obesity adjacent population.
entries.thesisLong:
Dexcom is the CGM category leader. 2025 revenue grew 16% to $4.662B (15% organic), with US +11% and international +18%. Management guided 2026 to $5.16–5.25B (+11–13%). Approximately 74% US CGM share gives Dexcom near-utility status in the Type 1 and intensive-insulin Type 2 segments.

The G7 15-Day System, launched broadly in 2025, extends sensor wear from 10 to 15 days — meaningfully improving reimbursement economics and patient experience versus Abbott's FreeStyle Libre. The Stelo over-the-counter sensor (cleared by FDA in 2024) opened a new wedge into non-insulin Type 2 and adjacent wellness/obesity use cases, where GLP-1 patients increasingly use CGMs to track metabolic response.

The TAM is being recast upward. The global CGM market is on a path to $47B+, and Dexcom is investing in international expansion (notably Japan, Korea, Brazil, India) and in software (Dexcom ONE+, partnership with Oura).

The bottleneck story: CGM sensor manufacturing requires high-precision enzyme deposition, complex multi-layer fabrication, and validated supply chains that take years to certify. Only Dexcom, Abbott, and Medtronic ship at scale. The risks are share loss to Abbott Libre 3 in cost-sensitive markets, GLP-1-driven Type 2 prevalence reductions over time, and Medicare DME reimbursement changes — but in 2026 Dexcom remains the chokepoint name on real-time glucose data.
catalysts: Stelo OTC scale into prediabetes and GLP-1 users
International expansion in Japan, Korea, Brazil, India
G7 15-Day reimbursement uptake
Type 2 non-insulin coverage expansions
Software / pump-integration partnerships
risks: Abbott FreeStyle Libre 3 share gains
Medicare DME reimbursement headwinds
GLP-1 success reducing diabetes prevalence over time

entries.name: TAVR Sapien & Transcatheter Mitral/Tricuspid
entries.thesisShort: Edwards holds ~72% US TAVR share with the Sapien platform driving $4.5B in 2025 sales, while TMTT (Pascal, Evoque, Sapien M3) just grew 62% to a $134M run-rate and is guided to $740-780M in 2026.
entries.thesisLong:
Edwards Lifesciences is the structural heart category leader. Sapien TAVR holds ~72.3% US share in 2025 with full-year segment sales of $4.5B and 2026 guidance of $4.6–4.9B (+6–8%). Sapien is the most-studied TAVR valve with 15+ years of clinical data, 10 NEJM publications, and 1.2M+ patients treated globally — the gold-standard install base.

TMTT (Transcatheter Mitral and Tricuspid Therapies) is the explosive growth segment. 2025 TMTT sales hit $134.5M, up 61.9% YoY, and 2026 guidance calls for $740–780M (+35–45%). The segment includes Pascal (mitral repair), Evoque (tricuspid replacement), and the just-approved Sapien M3 (mitral replacement). Long-term targets put TMTT at $2B by 2030.

The bottleneck is structural: transcatheter heart valve approvals require massive multi-year RCTs (PARTNER program for TAVR), training of interventional cardiology / structural heart programs, and procedural reimbursement infrastructure. Only Edwards and Medtronic compete in TAVR at scale; Abbott (MitraClip) and Edwards are the duopoly in mitral repair; Edwards is essentially alone in tricuspid replacement with Evoque.

The risks are mid-term TAVR mature-market share normalization (Medtronic Evolut FX and Abbott Navitor pushing back), execution on TMTT clinical ramp, and reimbursement scrutiny on Evoque tricuspid. But on the chokepoint map for structural heart, Edwards is the dominant name through the rest of the decade.
catalysts: Sapien M3 mitral replacement commercial launch
Evoque tricuspid market education and adoption
TAVR moderate AS / asymptomatic indication expansion
International TAVR penetration
PASCAL Precision iterative launches
risks: Medtronic Evolut FX share recovery in TAVR
Abbott Navitor and TriClip competitive pressure
Reimbursement tightening on novel TMTT procedures

entries.name: da Vinci Robotic Surgery Platform
entries.thesisShort: Intuitive Surgical's da Vinci is the global standard for soft-tissue robotic surgery with 11,106 systems installed worldwide as of December 2025, and the da Vinci 5 ramp drove a 12% installed-base expansion in a single year.
entries.thesisLong:
Intuitive Surgical owns soft-tissue robotic surgery. The da Vinci installed base reached 11,106 systems at year-end 2025 (+12% YoY), and 2025 placements totaled 1,721 systems, of which 870 were the next-generation da Vinci 5 — up from 362 in 2024. Full year 2025 revenue hit $10.06B (+21%).

The moat is multi-layered: 25 years of clinical data across urology, gynecology, general surgery, and thoracic; a 2M+ procedure-per-year recurring instruments and accessories revenue stream (the razor-blade economics); deeply trained surgeon population with multi-year learning curves; and integrated training and simulation infrastructure that hospitals built around da Vinci.

The da Vinci 5 transition is the most important platform refresh in a decade. Force feedback, 10,000x compute headroom for AI, and improved imaging make it the upgrade path for the entire installed base. SP (single-port) extends the franchise into transoral, transanal, and other narrow-corridor procedures that multi-port can't reach.

Competition is finally real but contained. Medtronic Hugo is rolling out internationally; Stryker is extending Mako into soft tissue; J&J Ottava is approaching first-in-human. None have the procedure breadth, instrument library, or surgeon network that da Vinci has compounded over 25 years. Risks are tariff exposure on Chinese-made components, Hugo's price-aggressive entry into emerging markets, and any meaningful da Vinci 5 ramp execution stumble — but Intuitive remains the textbook chokepoint name in surgical robotics.
catalysts: da Vinci 5 ramp into existing installed base
SP indication expansion in colorectal and urology
International (Japan, India, Korea) penetration
AI-enhanced surgical analytics monetization
Outpatient surgery channel expansion
risks: Medtronic Hugo gaining international beachheads
J&J Ottava entering clinical use
Tariffs on China-sourced componentry

entries.name: Mako Orthopedic Robotics
entries.thesisShort: Stryker's Mako has 3,000+ installations and 2M+ procedures across 46 countries, and the new handheld Mako RPS extends robotic-assist into a much larger surgeon population than the bulky main system can reach.
entries.thesisLong:
Stryker's Mako is the dominant orthopedic surgical robot. 3,000+ Mako platform installations globally and 2M+ cumulative procedures across 46 countries make it the procedural standard in robot-assisted total knee, partial knee, and total hip arthroplasty. Record installation quarters in 2025 reflect ongoing share capture from Zimmer (Rosa) and J&J (Velys).

The pull-through economics are the moat. Hospitals that buy a Mako system commit to Stryker's implant ecosystem (Triathlon knees, Insignia hips, Tritanium acetabular cups) — and switching surgeons off a system they trained on is exceptionally difficult. Mako installs drive multi-year implant share gains in every account.

The Mako RPS (Robotic Power System) handheld launch in early 2026 is a strategic expansion. Where the main Mako requires a dedicated robot bay, Mako RPS is a handheld robotic device that extends robotic precision to ambulatory surgery centers (ASCs) and lower-volume hospitals — potentially doubling the addressable surgical population. Limited market release is underway with full launch through 2026.

The global orthopedic surgical robotics market is projected to grow from $13.7B in 2025 to $27.1B by 2030 (14.7% CAGR), and Stryker is the share leader. Risks are competition from J&J Velys and Zimmer Rosa in price-sensitive accounts, ASC migration shifting reimbursement, and any safety event with the new handheld platform — but Mako is the chokepoint franchise on which the rest of Stryker's MedSurg business compounds.
catalysts: Mako RPS handheld full commercial launch
ASC channel expansion driving placement velocity
International (Japan, China, Latin America) growth
Insignia hip and Triathlon knee pull-through
Spine and shoulder Mako applications
risks: J&J Velys and Zimmer Rosa competitive pressure
ASC reimbursement shifts compressing capital sales
Slower than modeled Mako RPS adoption

entries.name: Austedo & Biosimilars Engine
entries.thesisShort: Teva grew to $17.3B in 2025 revenue across 11 consecutive quarters of growth, with Austedo hitting $2.2B (+35%) and a biosimilar portfolio targeting double-revenue by 2027.
entries.thesisLong:
Teva is the generics-to-innovative pivot story. 2025 revenue of $17.3B reflected 11 consecutive quarters of growth as the Pivot to Growth strategy under CEO Richard Francis worked through the system. Austedo (deutetrabenazine for Huntington's chorea and tardive dyskinesia) hit $2.2B in 2025 (+35%) and is the franchise leading the innovative transition.

The core generics business is mature and pressured: global generics declined 2% in local currency, with US generics down 6%, Europe +1%, International -1%. But that mix is now less than half of revenue, with innovative (Austedo, Ajovy migraine, Uzedy long-acting risperidone) and biosimilars carrying the growth.

Biosimilars are the quiet wedge. Teva is targeting biosimilar revenue doubling by 2027 with launches across Humira, Stelara, Prolia (denosumab), and others. The portfolio leverages Teva's existing complex-generic manufacturing scale and supply-chain footprint that few competitors can match.

The near-term setback is 2026 guidance: Teva guided $16.4–16.8B, signaling a step-down from 2025 driven by US generic erosion and select LOEs. The longer story is whether Austedo growth + biosimilar ramp can offset the generics drag and make Teva a compounded mid-single-digit revenue grower. On the chokepoint map, Teva remains the largest pure-play generics + biosimilar manufacturer globally — a structural utility for affordable medicine access that any drug-pricing reform tailwind benefits.
catalysts: Austedo XR uptake and TD label expansion
Biosimilar Stelara, Prolia, Humira launches
Uzedy long-acting risperidone share growth
Debt paydown improving leverage profile
Olanzapine LAI Phase 3 readout
risks: US generics pricing pressure persisting
Austedo growth deceleration
Drug pricing reform compressing biosimilar economics

entries.name: Direct-to-Consumer Telehealth Platform
entries.thesisShort: Hims hit 2.5M subscribers and $2.35B revenue in 2025, then pivoted hard in early 2026 from compounded GLP-1s into a Wegovy distribution role with Novo and a LillyDirect routing arrangement for Zepbound.
entries.thesisLong:
Hims & Hers built the largest consumer-direct telehealth platform in the US: 2.5M subscribers at year-end 2025 (+282K YoY) and $2.35B in revenue (up from $1.5B in 2024). The growth was juiced by compounded GLP-1s, which contributed roughly $420M of H1 2025 sales (~38% of revenue), but that line collapsed when FDA shortage-list status ended for semaglutide and tirzepatide.

The February 2026 reset was decisive. FDA, HHS, and Novo Nordisk all moved against Hims' compounding strategy in a single week. Hims pulled the $49 oral semaglutide pill and pivoted to a Wegovy distribution arrangement with Novo plus LillyDirect routing for Zepbound and orforglipron — converting from compounding pirate to legitimate branded distribution channel.

The core platform underneath remains valuable: hair, sexual health, mental health, dermatology, and weight loss verticals all subscribe at scale; ~95% of subscribers are not on GLP-1s; the Eucalyptus acquisition extended the platform internationally. The peptide pipeline (testosterone, NAD+, longevity peptides) is the next compounded category but carries its own regulatory risk.

The chokepoint framing is unique: Hims doesn't gate any drug supply, but it gates patient acquisition cost and direct-to-consumer Rx workflow at a scale (millions of subscribers, in-house pharmacy, telemedicine network across all 50 states) that branded pharma now needs as a distribution partner. Whether the platform can grow without compounded GLP-1 economics is the 2026 question.
catalysts: Wegovy distribution partnership scaling
LillyDirect routing for Zepbound and orforglipron
Peptide and longevity vertical launches
Eucalyptus international expansion
Mental health and dermatology subscriber growth
risks: GLP-1 revenue replacement gap into 2026
FDA scrutiny of compounded peptides
CAC inflation in non-GLP-1 verticals
Competition from Amazon Pharmacy and LillyDirect direct

entries.name: Plasma-Derived Immunoglobulins
entries.thesisShort: Grifols' immunoglobulin franchise grew 14.7% constant-currency to lead $7.5B in 2025 revenue, with subcutaneous Xembify up 60% and plasma collection volumes rising 8% industry-wide.
entries.thesisLong:
Grifols sits at one end of an oligopoly that gates plasma-derived therapies. 2025 revenue of EUR 7.524B grew 7% constant currency, with the immunoglobulin (IG) franchise growing 14.7% CC and subcutaneous Xembify surging 59.5% YoY. Group profit more than doubled to EUR 402M.

The plasma chokepoint is real and difficult to displace. IVIG and SCIG (intravenous and subcutaneous immunoglobulins) are used in primary immune deficiencies, CIDP, ITP, and multifocal motor neuropathy. The supply chain requires 1,000+ paid-donor plasma collection centers globally (Grifols, CSL Behring, Takeda dominate), 9-12 month plasma-to-product lead times, and FDA-licensed fractionation plants. New entrants face a multi-year build-out before any commercial volume.

Industry plasma collection volumes grew 8% in 2025, easing the pandemic-era supply shortage. Strategic moves to widen plasma access include Grifols' EMA-approved Egypt arrangement and its Canadian Blood Services partnership in Canada (the world's fourth-largest IgG market). Shanghai RAAS partnership manages China dynamics.

The near-term overhang is the albumin segment (-5.1% in 2025) on China pricing pressure, plus the lingering balance-sheet questions from the post-Brookfield bid period. But the core IG growth engine, the expanded plasma footprint, and the structural supply-side moat make Grifols the clearest public way to play the plasma chokepoint after Takeda's diversification and CSL's Australian listing.
catalysts: Xembify subcutaneous IG continued share gains
Egypt and Canada plasma collection scaling
Fibrinogen approval ramp
Albumin China pricing stabilization
Debt refinancing improving capital structure
risks: China albumin pricing further deterioration
FcRn antagonists (efgartigimod) eating IG indications
Donor compensation regulation changes

entries.name: Companion Animal Pharmaceuticals
entries.thesisShort: Zoetis is the global animal-health leader with $9.35B in 2025 revenue and 70% companion-animal mix, anchored by the Apoquel/Cytopoint dermatology franchise and a recovering Librela osteoarthritis biologic.
entries.thesisLong:
Zoetis is the only public pure-play global animal-health leader at scale. 2025 revenue hit ~$9.35B (US $5.1B, International $4.25B), with companion animal at ~70% of mix and livestock at ~29%. The recurring nature of pet pharma — chronic dermatology, OA pain, parasiticides, vaccines — produces consistent mid-single-digit organic growth with FDA-class margins.

The Key Dermatology franchise (Apoquel, Apoquel Chewable, Cytopoint) hit $608M in 2025, +10% operationally. Apoquel/Apoquel Chewable alone is roughly 12% of total revenue — the kind of single-product franchise that defines the moat. Parasiticides (Simparica Trio in dogs, Revolution Plus in cats) and vaccines round out the companion portfolio.

Librela (anti-NGF monoclonal antibody for canine OA pain) had a tough 2025: US sales -16%, with the broader OA-pain mAb segment -12% on safety-perception headwinds and slower vet adoption than originally guided. Zoetis is investing in vet education and label clarification to restore growth in 2026.

The chokepoint framing: Zoetis owns the relationship with vet clinics. Sales reps, training programs, diagnostic integration, and decades of clinical data make displacement extraordinarily difficult — and the industry duopoly with Elanco gives Zoetis pricing discipline through the cycle. Risks are Librela ramp slower than modeled, generic Apoquel exposure post-LOE, and pet-spend cyclicality, but on the bottleneck question for animal health innovation, Zoetis is the name.
catalysts: Librela US commercial reset and education ramp
Apoquel Chewable continued share gains
Simparica Trio international expansion
Solensia (cat OA) growth
Pet diagnostic and AI integration partnerships
risks: Librela safety-perception persistence
Apoquel LOE approaching with generic threat
Pet-spend recession sensitivity

entries.name: Acute Care Hospital Network
entries.thesisShort: HCA generated $75.6B in 2025 revenue across 190 hospitals and ~2,500 ambulatory sites, with a 27% market share target rising to 29% by 2030 in its core MSAs.
entries.thesisLong:
HCA Healthcare is the largest for-profit hospital operator in the US and the volume-share leader in most of its core markets. 2025 revenue of $75.6B (up from $70.6B in 2024) reflected 190 hospitals and ~2,500 ambulatory sites of care across 19 states and the UK. 2026 revenue is guided to $76.5–80B.

The market-share thesis is the chokepoint. HCA targets 29% share in its addressable markets by 2030, up from 27% today. Geographic clustering (Florida, Texas, Tennessee, Virginia, Colorado) creates network effects: physician recruitment, payer contracting leverage, and capex efficiency that smaller systems can't match. The ambulatory build-out (freestanding ERs, urgent care, ASCs, physician clinics) extends the funnel into the hospital and protects against site-of-care shifts.

A $10B share repurchase program announced in early 2026 reflects management's confidence in cash generation. The model carries leverage but funds it with predictable hospital EBITDA in concentrated markets where HCA is often the largest employer.

The risk profile is policy-heavy: any meaningful change to commercial-rate negotiating power, 340B drug pricing, Medicaid expansion rollback, or site-of-service payment parity would compress margins. Labor inflation and physician practice consolidation also remain pressures. But on the question of who controls acute-care delivery in the highest-growth US MSAs, HCA is the chokepoint operator with no comparable scale challenger — a defensive infrastructure asset masquerading as a healthcare equity.
catalysts: $10B share repurchase execution
Ambulatory site expansion across core MSAs
Commercial payer rate increases for 2026 contracts
Trauma and tertiary referral volume growth
International (UK) capacity additions
risks: Medicaid expansion rollback in red states
Site-of-service payment parity legislation
Labor cost re-acceleration
340B program restrictions
